prompt.context: SKP (Simon-Kucher & Partners) has been retained by Vivid, a consumer electronics screen manufacturer, to perform a pricing optimization project. Vivid's main product is HDTV screens. Its main customers are well-known TV manufacturers in Asia and the US, who buy other components, build finished TVs, and sell them to retailers who use global distribution channels to reach end-users. You have been assigned to this team and today is your first meeting with the project manager to review the information collected and brainstorm about key hypotheses.
prompt.question: Review the information collected on Vivid's pricing and supply chain situation, identify pricing opportunities, and provide actionable recommendations to grow revenue.

clarifying_info.q: Is Vivid concerned about profitability, or just revenue?
clarifying_info.a: The client is looking at pricing in search of opportunities to grow revenue.
Vivid technology is patent-protected, and for manufacturers to switch suppliers would require costly plant reconfiguration.
While sales volumes have been increasing, revenue has remained flat.

clarifying_info.q: Are competitors experiencing the same revenue decline?
clarifying_info.a: Unfortunately, we don't have financials for any of the competitors.

exhibits.title: Discount/Volume Curve
exhibits.shows: A scatter plot of individual sales contracts, with Discount (%) on the x-axis ranging from roughly 35% to 50% and Volume (units) on the y-axis ranging from 0 to 5,500. List price is noted as $400/unit.
exhibits.data: x-axis: Discount % from ~35% to ~50%; y-axis: Volume units from 0 to 5,500; visible cluster/peak around 40% discount; many points at or above 40% discount; list price $400/unit

exhibits.title: Internal/External Interviews
exhibits.shows: Excerpts from interviews with TV manufacturer customers and Vivid's internal sales team.
exhibits.data: Customer quotes: (1) 'Although other screen technologies are cheaper, this product gives the quality we need to charge the prices we charge on the street.' (2) 'We built a $1 billion plant to produce HDTVs this year. The plan only works with VIVID's screens.' Internal sales quotes: (1) 'Although we have discount floors in the TV division, when we are getting closer to the end of the quarter, I need to close the deals to reach my sales quota. The competition is too strong in this market and I need to give the discounts.' (2) 'We can give higher discounts every year because our costs go down every year too.' (3) 'If the management keeps asking us to grow our market share, we need to lower our prices to increase our sales, it is the law of demand, basic economics!'

framework: Pricing/Profit: price level, price metric, price structure, discounting policy, discounting levels, WTP, segmentation
Sales: sales volumes, sales incentives, sales KPIs, discounting data, trends
Customers: customer feedback, switching costs, supply chain role, quantity
Product: features, quality, relative performance, comparative pricing/benchmarking
Competition: market shares, substitutes, competitors' pricing

questions.prompt: Production costs have been: 2015 $400/screen, 2016 $250/screen, 2017 $200/screen, 2018 (forecast) $180/screen. The retail street price has been $1,000/screen each year. What can you draw from this?
questions.guidance: Candidate should note that Vivid has realized significant but decreasing economies of scale (37.5%, 20%, 10% cost savings year over year). Profit margins have increased across the value chain each year. However, the wholesale price is still needed to assess Vivid's own profitability. The rate of cost reduction is slowing, meaning continued heavy discounting will become unsustainable.

questions.prompt: Marketing has set a list price of $400/screen and a discount authority floor of 40% for the sales team. Exhibit 1 shows contract prices vs. volumes. What do you see?
questions.guidance: Candidate should observe: (1) Almost 40% of sales violates the 40% discount floor — salespeople are discounting beyond their authority. (2) There is a peak cluster at exactly the 40% floor — salespeople discount to the maximum allowed. This suggests a volume-based sales incentive is driving price erosion. Vivid should consider adding a profit-based component to sales compensation. If time allows, calculate the weighted average selling price.

math.setup: Four discount tiers visible: 50%, 45%, 40%, 35%. List price = $400/unit. Compute selling price per tier, then weight by volume to find average selling price.
steps: Volumes (read from exhibit): 3,000 units @ $200; 1,000 units @ $220; 5,000 units @ $240; 1,000 units @ $260

questions.prompt: The HDTV value chain has four players: Supplier (backlighting) with cost $200 and profit $20; Vivid (screens) with cost $200; TV Manufacturer with cost $300; Retailer with cost $150 and profit $30. The retail street price is $1,000. Using the average selling price calculated, what can you tell about the distribution of surplus in the supply chain and the TV manufacturer's willingness to pay?
questions.guidance: Candidate must compute Vivid's profit from its average ASP, then back-calculate the TV manufacturer's profit as the residual. Should note that Vivid retains only ~$28 of the $150 total supply chain profit, far less than the TV manufacturer's $72. This raises the question of whether Vivid should capture more value given its patent protection and customers' high switching costs.

math.setup: Use ASP of $228 and known cost/profit data to fill in the value chain and find TV manufacturer profit.
steps: Sum all known supply chain components: Supplier ($200+$20=$220) + Vivid ($200+$28=$228) + TV Manufacturer ($300+unknown) + Retailer ($150+$30=$180)
TV manufacturer profit: Retail price - subtotal = $1,000 - $928 = $72
math.answer: Vivid profit = $28/unit; TV manufacturer profit = $72/unit; total supply chain profit = $150/unit

questions.prompt: Exhibit 2 shows excerpts from customer and internal interviews. What can we take from this?
questions.guidance: Customer interviews reveal: high willingness-to-pay for Vivid's quality (customers can charge premium retail prices because of screen quality); very high switching costs (a $1 billion plant was built around Vivid's screens). Internal interviews reveal: salesforce is under volume quota pressure, causing end-of-quarter discounting beyond authorized floors; sales reps rationalize deeper discounts because costs decline annually; management's market-share growth directive misaligns with revenue optimization. Implication: clear opportunity for a price increase and need to restructure sales incentives.

brainstorming.prompt: We need to send a request for information to the client at the beginning of the project. What information do you think would be useful to ask for?

recommendation: Vivid should target a price increase: a $40/$60 split of the $100 surplus between Vivid and the TV manufacturer (i.e., Vivid takes $40 profit and TV manufacturer takes $60) would give both players a 20% return on sales, implying a Vivid target ASP of $240
Vivid should overhaul its sales compensation structure by introducing a profit-based variable component alongside the current volume quota, to eliminate the incentive for excessive discounting
Vivid should implement a more granular discount authority system to prevent salespeople from discounting beyond the floor, particularly at end of quarter
risks: TV manufacturers may resist a price increase and attempt to find or develop alternative suppliers despite switching costs
If cost reductions slow further, the current discount culture will rapidly erode margins
Sales force morale or retention issues if compensation restructuring is perceived as punitive
next_steps: Model the revenue and margin impact of raising ASP from $228 to $240
Design a revised discount authority framework with tiered approval levels
Restructure sales compensation to include a profit margin component
Conduct further competitive analysis to quantify switching cost barriers and validate pricing power
